title: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding: triage, resuscitation, endoscopy

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the 2021 ACG upper gastrointestinal and ulcer bleeding guideline and AASLD variceal guidance. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: At or below what Glasgow-Blatchford score can a patient with upper GI bleeding be managed as an outpatient?
questions.why: The score uses urea, haemoglobin, blood pressure, pulse, melaena, syncope, and liver and cardiac disease. A score of 0 or 1 carries under 1% risk of needing intervention.

questions.q: Below what haemoglobin is transfusion recommended in upper GI bleeding without cardiovascular disease?
questions.why: A restrictive strategy improved survival in trials, partly because over-transfusion raises portal pressure in cirrhosis. With cardiovascular disease the threshold is 8.

questions.q: Within how many hours of presentation should endoscopy be performed for non-variceal upper GI bleeding?
questions.why: Resuscitation comes first; very early endoscopy in unstable patients did not improve outcomes. Suspected variceal bleeding is scoped within 12 hours.

questions.q: What is the role of an intravenous proton pump inhibitor before endoscopy?
questions.a: Reasonable to give; it reduces high-risk stigmata but does not change mortality
questions.why: After endoscopic treatment of a high-risk ulcer, high-dose PPI for 72 hours reduces rebleeding. Lower-risk lesions go straight to oral dosing.

questions.q: A patient with known cirrhosis presents with haematemesis. Which treatments are started before endoscopy?
a: Resuscitation to a haemoglobin of 7 to 8
d: Fresh frozen plasma to normalise the INR
questions.why: Antibiotics reduce infection, rebleeding and death in cirrhotic bleeders. Beta blockers come after the acute bleed, and the INR does not predict bleeding in cirrhosis.

questions.q: Which drug given 30 to 90 minutes before endoscopy improves the view by emptying the stomach?
questions.why: It acts as a motilin agonist and reduces the need for repeat endoscopy. Nasogastric lavage is no longer recommended for the same purpose.

questions.q: A bleeding ulcer is found. Which infection is tested for and treated?
questions.why: A negative test during an acute bleed can be false, so it is repeated later. Eradication is confirmed after treatment because untreated infection leads to rebleeding.

questions.q: A patient on aspirin for a prior myocardial infarction has a bleeding ulcer treated endoscopically. When does the aspirin restart?
questions.a: As soon as haemostasis is secure, usually within days
questions.why: Stopping aspirin for secondary prevention raised cardiovascular death in a randomised trial more than it reduced rebleeding. It restarts with a PPI alongside.

questions.q: Which laboratory finding points to an upper rather than lower source in a patient with red blood per rectum?
questions.a: A raised urea out of proportion to creatinine
questions.why: Digested blood raises the urea. A brisk upper bleed can present as haematochezia, and a raised urea with haemodynamic instability points to the upper tract.

questions.q: Endoscopy shows an ulcer with a clean base. What endoscopic treatment is needed?
questions.why: Clean-base and flat-spot ulcers rebleed rarely and can be fed and discharged early. Active bleeding, a visible vessel and an adherent clot are the lesions that get treated.

questions.q: An ulcer rebleeds after endoscopic therapy. What is the next step?
questions.why: If the second endoscopy fails, transcatheter embolisation is preferred over surgery in most centres. Surgery is for failure of both.

questions.q: After a bleeding duodenal ulcer, how long is oral proton pump inhibitor therapy continued for healing?
questions.why: Longer courses are for patients who must stay on NSAIDs or antiplatelets. Gastric ulcers get a repeat endoscopy to confirm healing and exclude malignancy.
